screens.title: Malware Analysis & Reverse Engineering Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn the foundational skills to analyze malicious software safely and extract meaningful intelligence. We begin by learning two complementary approaches: static analysis, which inspects files without running them, and dynamic analysis, which executes samples inside a protected, isolated environment to observe real behavior. You will also learn how to prepare a VM with snapshots and network simulation tools so you never risk your production environment. Practical tools appear throughout: string extractors, disassemblers such as Ghidra or IDA Pro, dependency viewers, process monitors, A P I loggers, and debuggers. A concrete scenario we will use is a suspected ransomware sample called invoice. exe — you will see how to gather its file type and hashes, extract strings that hint at targeted file types or C2, and then run it in an isolated VM to capture file system changes and network beaconing. Finally, reverse engineering techniques and unpacking strategies show you how to reach the original code when packing or obfuscation is present. After this chapter you should be able to produce actionable IoCs, document findings, and know when to escalate to threat intelligence or incident response. Consider: what single artifact would you prioritize first when you find a suspicious executable in your environment?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter has specific, measurable objectives that focus your learning. First, you'll be able to distinguish static from dynamic analysis. Static techniques let you inspect files safely without execution, while dynamic techniques reveal runtime behavior; understanding the difference helps you choose the right first step. Second, you'll know how to set up an isolated VM environment with snapshots, network simulation, and monitoring tools so you avoid infecting production systems. Third, you'll learn to use common static tools such as string extractors, file type identifiers, and disassemblers to gather initial intelligence like imports and suspicious strings. Fourth, you'll perform controlled dynamic analysis to observe file and registry changes, A P I calls, and network traffic so you can produce actionable IoCs. Each objective is tied to practical outcomes: safer labs, better triage, and concrete artifacts you can feed into detection systems. Practice these skills in sequence and keep detailed notes; documentation is itself an objective because it enables reproducible, defensible findings.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Advanced Tasks
screens.narratorSegment: These additional objectives take the basics deeper. You will gain a working familiarity with disassemblers and decompilers so you can identify functions, imports, and likely behavior from static code. You will learn how to operate debuggers to step through code, find the original entry point in packed samples, and capture memory-resident unpacked code. You will also identify common obfuscation techniques—string encryption, A P I hashing, and control-flow flattening—and practice methods to reveal them. Finally, you'll practice extracting and documenting three classes of IoCs: file hashes and file paths, network indicators such as domains and IPs, and host artifacts like new registry keys, file extensions used by ransomware, and mutex names. Each objective emphasizes safe handling, repeatable methods, and good documentation because the value of analysis is not only knowledge but the ability to share and operationalize that intelligence.

screens.title: What is Malware Analysis?
screens.narratorSegment: Malware analysis is the disciplined process of studying malicious software to understand what it does, how it works, where it came from, and how to detect it. This extends beyond curiosity: a concrete outcome is a set of indicators of compromise you can operationalize in SIEM and EDR tools. Start by forming a hypothesis about the sample—what category might it belong to, does it appear to target files, or does it seem stealthy and network-aware? For example, a binary that calls networking APIs and creates new files could be a downloader or ransomware. A common misconception is to treat analysis as a one-step activity; instead, it's iterative: initial static clues guide safe dynamic tests, which in turn inform deeper reverse engineering. Practice documentation from the first step: capture file hashes, sample metadata, and the environment you used. That record makes your findings reproducible and valuable to other teams. Consider: which artifact — a file hash, a domain, or a registry key — would give your defenders the fastest edge if you shared it first? What is Malware Analysis? means malware analysis is an iterative process that produces actionable iocs and a clear explanation of malicious behavior.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and practical outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › What is Malware Analysis?
Malware Analysis: A practical definition
Study of malicious software to determine capabilities, origin, and indicators you can act on.
  • • Produce IoCs to feed detection systems.
  • • Decide if static inspection suffices or a dynamic run is needed.
  • • Document environment and steps for reproducibility.
  • • Iterate: static clues guide runtime tests and reverse engineering.
Key Takeaway

Malware analysis yields concrete artifacts (hashes, domains, registry keys) that improve detection and response.

Concrete example
An executable that imports networking libraries and writes files likely needs dynamic analysis to confirm whether it exfiltrates data or encrypts files.
Common misconception
Running a sample immediately is unsafe. Always collect static clues and prepare an isolated VM before any execution.
Analogy
Think of static analysis as reading a recipe, and dynamic analysis as tasting the finished dish inside a sealed kitchen.
Check
If a file is packed or strings are encrypted, static analysis may not reveal intent; plan for debugging and unpacking.

screens.title: Static vs Dynamic Analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Static and dynamic analysis serve different but complementary roles. Static analysis inspects the file without running it: strings extraction, file header checks, import tables, and disassembly. The main advantage is safety: you never execute the sample, so there's zero risk to your host from the sample itself. The drawback is obvious: modern malware often uses packing, encryption, or A P I hashing to hide behavior. Dynamic analysis executes the sample inside a controlled, isolated environment so you can observe actual runtime behavior like file system modifications, registry persistence, process injection, and network beaconing. This reveals the malware's true actions but introduces risk if isolation is imperfect. A common workflow is to start static to build hypotheses—extract strings, check imports, and identify packers—and only then run dynamic analysis to confirm behavior. For example, if strings show references to file extensions and encryption APIs, dynamic execution with test files can confirm ransomware behavior. A misconception is that dynamic analysis replaces static: in practice, both are required for confident conclusions. Which clue from static analysis would you trust enough to create an initial detection rule?

keyIdea.text: Static = safe but limited; dynamic = revealing but riskier. Use both iteratively to validate hypotheses.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Static vs Dynamic
Static Analysis
Safe inspection without execution.
  • • Tools: file, PEiD, strings, FLOSS, Ghidra/IDA imports.
  • • Finds: embedded URLs, mutex names, referenced APIs, packer signatures.
  • • Limitations: encrypted strings, packed sections, API hashing.
Example
A sample with imports for ws2_32.dll suggests networking capability; static clues point to possible C2 communication to verify dynamically.
Dynamic Analysis
Execute inside an isolated VM to watch behavior.
  • • Tools: Process Monitor, Wireshark, FakeNet-NG, API Monitor, Cuckoo.
  • • Observes: file encryption, registry persistence, process injection, network beaconing.
  • • Caution: always run in a fully isolated, snapshot-enabled VM.
Misconception
Dynamic analysis is not a substitute for static; packed samples often require both methods to reveal the original code.
Check your understanding
Name one static artifact that would prompt a dynamic run.
Pro tip
Collect hashes and a clean snapshot before any execution so you can rollback quickly after experiments.
Key Takeaway
Start safe with static; use dynamic to confirm and gather runtime IoCs.

screens.title: Safe Dynamic Analysis: Preparing an Isolated VM
screens.narratorSegment: Preparing an isolated environment is the most important safety task before executing malware. Begin by creating a dedicated analysis VM that is strictly separated from corporate networks; network interfaces should be disabled unless you intentionally simulate them. Take a clean snapshot before you run anything; snapshots let you return to a known good state quickly. Install monitoring tools inside the VM such as Process Monitor and Process Explorer to watch process and file activity, Wireshark for packet capture, and A P I logging tools or a sandbox like Cuckoo for deeper tracing. Use FakeNet-NG or INetSim when you need to observe network behavior without allowing outbound connections to real command-and-control infrastructure. Configure the VM with test files—common document types and sample folders—to detect encryption or deletion behavior. A common mistake is running analysis on a host machine or leaving shared folders enabled; those actions risk spreading infection. Finally, document the VM configuration and the snapshot ID; good notes make your experiments reproducible and defensible. What single VM configuration would you check first to ensure safety before executing a sample? Safe Dynamic Analysis: Preparing an Isolated VM means use isolated vms with snapshots, disabled host/network bridges, and simulated services to observe malware without risk.. In practical terms, essential steps to avoid cross-contamination and capture behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Safe Dynamic Analysis
VM Preparation Steps
  1. Build a dedicated analysis VM with no production access.
  2. Disable host networking or route through an isolated lab bridge.
  3. Install Process Monitor, Wireshark, and API logging tools.
  4. Create a clean snapshot before any execution.
  5. Use FakeNet-NG/INetSim to simulate network services when needed.
Monitoring & Safety
Place dummy documents in the VM to measure file-targeting behavior. Keep shared folders disabled to avoid accidental host infection.
Example Configuration
Snapshot labeled clean-0001, FakeNet-NG running on a private lab subnet, Process Monitor logging to file, Wireshark capturing to disk.
Common mistake
Leaving host-only or shared folders enabled; never use your workstation for analysis.
Key Takeaway
Isolation, snapshots, and simulated network services let you observe behavior safely and repeatably.

screens.title: Static Analysis Techniques and Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Static analysis gives you immediate, safe insight into a sample's structure. Begin with file-type identification using tools such as file on Linux or PEiD on Windows to determine format and detect common packers. Calculate hashes like SHA256 as the first IoC. Next, extract printable strings with tools like strings or FLOSS; these often reveal filenames, URLs, error messages, or A P I names and are quick wins. Inspect the import table and dependencies using Dependency Walker or Ghidra's import view to see which libraries are used—imports from ws2_32 are a hint the sample uses networking, while kernel32 imports suggest file system activity. If the import table is sparse or the binary is packed, suspect obfuscation and plan for unpacking. Finally, open the sample in a disassembler; even if code is obfuscated, function names, constants, and control-flow patterns convey important clues. A typical mistake is to stop at strings; while helpful, strings alone rarely prove functionality. Combine them with imports and disassembly to build a working hypothesis. Static Analysis Techniques and Tools means use file identifiers, string extraction, dependency viewers, and disassemblers to build an initial hypothesis about malware behavior.. In practical terms, file identification, strings, import tables, and packer detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Static Analysis Techniques
Core Static Steps
  • • File type and packer identification (file, PEiD).
  • • Hashing for IoC (SHA256).
  • • String extraction (strings, FLOSS).
  • • Import/dependency analysis (Dependency Walker, Ghidra).
  • • Disassembly to inspect code flow (Ghidra/IDA).
Example output
strings invoice.exe
---> "README.txt"
---> "CreateFile"
---> "ws2_32.dll"
---> "C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\Invoices"
Interpreting clues
A reference to README.txt and file APIs suggests dropping a ransom note or manipulating files; networking imports indicate possible C2 or data exfiltration.
Common mistake
Assuming obvious strings prove full behavior. Always confirm with imports, disassembly, or dynamic testing.
Pro tip
Always compute and record hashes before any analysis so you can reference the sample reliably.
Key Takeaway
Static tools provide safe, fast clues — packers and obfuscation often require debugger-assisted unpacking.

screens.title: Using Disassemblers: Ghidra & IDA
screens.narratorSegment: Disassemblers convert machine code into assembly and sometimes pseudo-code, letting you inspect logical structure without needing source code. Tools like Ghidra and IDA Pro give you the ability to list imports, identify functions, and see call graphs that highlight suspicious routines. Start by loading the binary and looking at the import table to find networking and cryptography libraries; then find functions that call those imports. Use cross-references to map where data moves. An example: if you find a function that calls CreateFile, WriteFile, and then a cryptographic function, that sequence suggests file encryption behavior. A misconception is to rely entirely on automatic decompilation—decompilers can mislabel functions or produce incorrect pseudo-code for obfuscated binaries; use the assembly and cross-references to verify critical behavior. In practice, disassembly narrows your dynamic tests: pick a function to break on in a debugger or force specific inputs to watch how the code behaves at runtime. Which import would you prioritize for creating a focused dynamic test? Using Disassemblers: Ghidra & IDA means use imports and call graphs to locate suspect functions and validate decompiler output against assembly and cross-references.. In practical terms, how to inspect imports, functions, and control flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Disassemblers
Inspecting Imports & Functions
Load the binary, examine the import table, and view cross-references to find where imports are used.
// Pseudo decompiler snippet
function do_encrypt() {
  open_file();         // CreateFile
  read_contents();
  call_crypto_api();   // CryptEncrypt
  write_encrypted();   // WriteFile
}
Cross-reference the crypto call to see which files are passed; that gives you file patterns to watch during dynamic runs.
Practical tips
  • • Verify decompiler output against the raw assembly.
  • • Use call-graph and function-size heuristics to find packing stubs.
  • • Label functions you confirm to speed later navigation.
Common misconception
Decompilers are infallible. They are tools that reduce effort; you must validate their output with assembly and runtime observations.

screens.title: Dynamic Analysis: Observing Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Dynamic analysis reveals what malware actually does when executed. Once your isolated VM and monitoring tools are ready, execute the sample and capture process events, file and registry modifications, and network traffic. Use Process Monitor or Process Explorer to capture process creation, parent-child relationships, and any process injection behavior. Look for suspicious file operations: mass renaming, deletion, or creation of encrypted file extensions, and the addition of ransom note files. For registry activity, watch Run and RunOnce keys, service creation entries, or modifications to shell values used for persistence. For network behavior, capture traffic with Wireshark while FakeNet-NG provides safe responses; identify DNS lookups, HTTP requests, or unexpected protocols and record destination domains or IP addresses as IoCs. A P I monitors or sandbox logs can provide a sequence of A P I calls that explain how the malware achieves a goal. A common misconception is to treat a single run as definitive; run samples multiple times and with small variations (different test files) to observe full behavior. What A P I call sequence would most strongly indicate file encryption?

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Dynamic Analysis
What to capture
Process Activity
Process creation, injections, parent/child chains, and suspicious names.
Filesystem & Registry
File writes/renames/deletions, Run keys, scheduled tasks, and persistence artifacts.
Network Traffic
DNS queries, HTTP requests, and outbound connections captured by Wireshark and controlled by FakeNet-NG.
API Calls
Sequence of system calls that reveal technique: file IO, crypto, network.
Example
Observe CreateFile -> ReadFile -> CryptEncrypt -> WriteFile to confirm encryption behavior, and capture any network beaconing that follows.
Practical cards
Checklist
Snapshot taken, Procmon logging, Wireshark capture, FakeNet active, test files present.
Common mistake
Not using simulated network services; malware may fail to demonstrate behavior if it expects C2 responses.
Key Takeaway
Multiple runs and controlled inputs reveal fuller behavior than a single, unmonitored execution.

screens.title: Monitoring Toolset: Procmon, Wireshark, FakeNet, and Sandboxes
screens.narratorSegment: A robust analysis architecture combines observability at multiple layers. Process Monitor and Process Explorer capture file, registry, and process events in real time, giving you a timeline of actions the sample performs. Wireshark provides packet-level capture to detect DNS queries, HTTP requests, and any exfiltration attempts. FakeNet-NG or INetSim sits between the sample and the real network to safely emulate DNS, HTTP, and other services — it prevents outbound connections from reaching real infrastructure while logging requested domains and content. A P I monitoring tools and sandboxes like Cuckoo can record higher-level A P I calls and produce structured logs. Use these tools together: for example, a DNS query logged by Wireshark and FakeNet-NG can be cross-referenced with a Process Monitor event to identify which process initiated communication. A common mistake is relying on a single tool; network and host visibility together produce the most actionable IoCs. Always synchronize clocks and collect file hashes so you can correlate logs across tools during analysis. Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Monitoring Toolset
Tool Roles
Procmon
Tracks processes, files, and registry modifications in detail.
Wireshark
Sniffs network packets for DNS, HTTP, and TCP/UDP traffic analysis.
FakeNet-NG
Simulates network services to safely observe malware behavior without reaching the internet.
Correlate logs: record timestamps, process IDs, and file hashes so you can link a network call in Wireshark back to the originating process and the file that was modified.
Example correlation
Wireshark shows a DNS lookup for bad.example; FakeNet logs the request and returns a controlled IP; Procmon shows the process that issued the DNS query. Together they form a reliable network IoC and process attribution.
Key Takeaway
Use multiple observability layers and precise timestamps to produce correlated, actionable intelligence.

screens.title: Debuggers and Unpacking Packed Samples
screens.narratorSegment: Packed or obfuscated samples hide the original code until runtime. A debugger lets you step through execution, set breakpoints, and observe the memory state where the unpacked code resides. Common debuggers include x64dbg, OllyDbg, and GDB. The typical approach is to run the sample under a debugger, set breakpoints on APIs often used by packers (for example, memory allocation and memory-protection APIs), then single-step until you find the original entry point. Once the unpacking routine has finished, dump the process memory to extract the unpacked binary for later static analysis. This approach requires careful planning: some malware detects debuggers and changes behavior, so prepare anti-anti-debug techniques or controlled inputs. A frequent misconception is that unpacking always yields fully legible code; sometimes additional deobfuscation is necessary. The major payoff is that unpacking converts a static dead end into analyzable code, enabling identification of functions like CreateRemoteThread or InternetOpenUrl that reveal capabilities. How would you verify your memory dump contains the correct original entry point? Debuggers and Unpacking Packed Samples means use debuggers to observe and dump unpacked memory, then analyze that dump in a disassembler to reveal hidden functionality.. In practical terms, using debuggers to observe unpacking routines and reach the original code. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › Debuggers & Unpacking
Debugger workflow
  1. Run sample under debugger in isolated VM.
  2. Set breakpoints on memory APIs and packer routines.
  3. Step until unpacking finishes and original code is in memory.
  4. Dump process memory and load into a disassembler for analysis.
Example functions to watch
VirtualAlloc, VirtualProtect, CreateRemoteThread — their usage can indicate unpacking or process injection.
Validation
Verify your dump by checking for valid PE headers and by confirming previously missing imports now appear. Load the dump into Ghidra or IDA to inspect functions.
Common mistake
Assuming a single dump captures everything. Some packers use multiple stages; you might need more than one dump point.
Pro tip
Label functions you confirm in the disassembler to speed later correlation with runtime logs.
Key Takeaway
Debugger-driven unpacking bridges the gap between opaque binaries and useful static analysis artifacts.

screens.title: Hands-on Workflow: invoice.exe (Suspected Ransomware)
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical workflow for a suspicious sample named invoice. exe. Start with static steps: identify the file type and compute hashes, for example using file and sha256sum to record a SHA256 fingerprint. Extract strings with strings or FLOSS to find ransom note markers, file extensions, or A P I names. Inspect imports with Dependency Walker or Ghidra to confirm use of file and network APIs. If static analysis suggests packing, plan to use a debugger later. For dynamic stages, prepare an isolated VM with a snapshot, enable Process Monitor, Wireshark, and FakeNet-NG, and place dummy documents to detect encryption. Execute invoice. exe while capturing Procmon and packet captures; watch for CreateFile/WriteFile sequences and registry changes for persistence. Finally, extract IoCs: file hashes, C2 domains or IPs, and host artifacts such as new Run keys or file extensions used for encryption. Document all steps and include timestamps so analysts can correlate logs. A common pitfall is skipping documentation; without it, IoCs lose context and value. Module 8 › Chapter 7.8 › invoice.exe Workflow
Static Steps (Example)
1) file / PEiD to identify PE and check packers. 2) sha256sum to record the hash. 3) strings or FLOSS to find filenames, ransom-note text, or API strings. 4) Dependency analysis to view imports like ws2_32 and kernel32.
# Example commands
file invoice.exe
sha256sum invoice.exe
strings invoice.exe | grep -i "README\|encrypt\|bitcoin"
Dynamic Setup & Execution
Prepare an isolated VM with a clean snapshot, install Procmon, Wireshark, and FakeNet. Place test documents. Start monitoring and then execute the sample. Capture process events, file writes and registry changes, and all network traffic.
Watch for CreateFile → ReadFile → CryptEncrypt → WriteFile sequences and for Run key additions indicating persistence.
IoC Extraction
File hashes (SHA256)
Network indicators (domains, IPs)
Host artifacts (registry keys, file paths, extensions)

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Assessment
screens.narratorSegment: Experienced analysts repeatedly encounter the same pitfalls. Don’t analyze samples on your production machine or leave shared folders enabled. Don’t skip static analysis before running a sample; static clues reduce risk and focus your experiments. Always document hashes, snapshots, and timestamps so your IoCs remain useful. When a sample is packed, use a debugger to step through the unpacking routine rather than relying on a public sandbox that might not reveal unpacked code. An illustrative assessment item asks which approach is most effective when a sample is packed: the correct choice is to use a debugger to step through runtime unpacking. That shows why understanding tools and methodology matters. Another important comparison is FakeNet-NG versus Wireshark: FakeNet intercepts and responds to network calls safely, while Wireshark captures the low-level packets for forensic analysis. Both are necessary for a full picture. As a quick test, ask yourself: when you find a packed executable in the wild, what is your three-step action plan? Common Pitfalls
  • • Analyzing on live infrastructure or with host shares open.
  • • Skipping static analysis before dynamic execution.
  • • Failing to document snapshots, hashes, and timestamps.
  • • Trusting public sandboxes for unpacking without validation.
Assessment sample
Question: A packed executable resists static inspection. Which is most effective? Answer: Use a debugger to step through runtime unpacking to observe the unpacked code and dump memory for later analysis.
Why this matters
Unpacking at runtime reveals the original code and imports, enabling accurate static analysis and IoC extraction.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Before you finish, keep three compact concepts in mind. First: static analysis is safe and fast, and it should be your starting point to collect hashes, strings, and import clues. Third: reverse engineering and debugging let you penetrate packing and obfuscation to reveal the original logic and produce higher-fidelity IoCs. Use these building blocks together: static clues shape your dynamic experiments, dynamic observations guide reverse-engineering focus, and all findings must be documented with timestamps and hashes so defenders can act. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn the foundational skills to analyze malicious software safely and extract meaningful intelligence. We begin by learning two complementary approaches: static analysis, which inspects files without running them, and dynamic analysis, which executes samples inside a protected, isolated environment to observe real behavior. You will also learn how to prepare a VM with snapshots and network simulation tools so you never risk your production environment. Practical tools appear throughout: string extractors, disassemblers such as Ghidra or IDA Pro, dependency viewers, process monitors, A P I loggers, and debuggers. A concrete scenario we will use is a suspected ransomware sample called invoice. exe — you will see how to gather its file type and hashes, extract strings that hint at targeted file types or C2, and then run it in an isolated VM to capture file system changes and network beaconing. Finally, reverse engineering techniques and unpacking strategies show you how to reach the original code when packing or obfuscation is present. After this chapter you should be able to produce actionable IoCs, document findings, and know when to escalate to threat intelligence or incident response. Consider: what single artifact would you prioritize first when you find a suspicious executable in your environment?

This chapter has specific, measurable objectives that focus your learning. First, you'll be able to distinguish static from dynamic analysis. Static techniques let you inspect files safely without execution, while dynamic techniques reveal runtime behavior; understanding the difference helps you choose the right first step. Second, you'll know how to set up an isolated VM environment with snapshots, network simulation, and monitoring tools so you avoid infecting production systems. Third, you'll learn to use common static tools such as string extractors, file type identifiers, and disassemblers to gather initial intelligence like imports and suspicious strings. Fourth, you'll perform controlled dynamic analysis to observe file and registry changes, A P I calls, and network traffic so you can produce actionable IoCs. Each objective is tied to practical outcomes: safer labs, better triage, and concrete artifacts you can feed into detection systems. Practice these skills in sequence and keep detailed notes; documentation is itself an objective because it enables reproducible, defensible findings.

These additional objectives take the basics deeper. You will gain a working familiarity with disassemblers and decompilers so you can identify functions, imports, and likely behavior from static code. You will learn how to operate debuggers to step through code, find the original entry point in packed samples, and capture memory-resident unpacked code. You will also identify common obfuscation techniques—string encryption, A P I hashing, and control-flow flattening—and practice methods to reveal them. Finally, you'll practice extracting and documenting three classes of IoCs: file hashes and file paths, network indicators such as domains and IPs, and host artifacts like new registry keys, file extensions used by ransomware, and mutex names. Each objective emphasizes safe handling, repeatable methods, and good documentation because the value of analysis is not only knowledge but the ability to share and operationalize that intelligence.

Malware analysis is the disciplined process of studying malicious software to understand what it does, how it works, where it came from, and how to detect it. This extends beyond curiosity: a concrete outcome is a set of indicators of compromise you can operationalize in SIEM and EDR tools. Start by forming a hypothesis about the sample—what category might it belong to, does it appear to target files, or does it seem stealthy and network-aware? For example, a binary that calls networking APIs and creates new files could be a downloader or ransomware. A common misconception is to treat analysis as a one-step activity; instead, it's iterative: initial static clues guide safe dynamic tests, which in turn inform deeper reverse engineering. Practice documentation from the first step: capture file hashes, sample metadata, and the environment you used. That record makes your findings reproducible and valuable to other teams. Consider: which artifact — a file hash, a domain, or a registry key — would give your defenders the fastest edge if you shared it first? What is Malware Analysis? means malware analysis is an iterative process that produces actionable iocs and a clear explanation of malicious behavior.. In practical terms, definition, purpose, and practical outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Static and dynamic analysis serve different but complementary roles. Static analysis inspects the file without running it: strings extraction, file header checks, import tables, and disassembly. The main advantage is safety: you never execute the sample, so there's zero risk to your host from the sample itself. The drawback is obvious: modern malware often uses packing, encryption, or A P I hashing to hide behavior. Dynamic analysis executes the sample inside a controlled, isolated environment so you can observe actual runtime behavior like file system modifications, registry persistence, process injection, and network beaconing. This reveals the malware's true actions but introduces risk if isolation is imperfect. A common workflow is to start static to build hypotheses—extract strings, check imports, and identify packers—and only then run dynamic analysis to confirm behavior. For example, if strings show references to file extensions and encryption APIs, dynamic execution with test files can confirm ransomware behavior. A misconception is that dynamic analysis replaces static: in practice, both are required for confident conclusions. Which clue from static analysis would you trust enough to create an initial detection rule?

Preparing an isolated environment is the most important safety task before executing malware. Begin by creating a dedicated analysis VM that is strictly separated from corporate networks; network interfaces should be disabled unless you intentionally simulate them. Take a clean snapshot before you run anything; snapshots let you return to a known good state quickly. Install monitoring tools inside the VM such as Process Monitor and Process Explorer to watch process and file activity, Wireshark for packet capture, and A P I logging tools or a sandbox like Cuckoo for deeper tracing. Use FakeNet-NG or INetSim when you need to observe network behavior without allowing outbound connections to real command-and-control infrastructure. Configure the VM with test files—common document types and sample folders—to detect encryption or deletion behavior. A common mistake is running analysis on a host machine or leaving shared folders enabled; those actions risk spreading infection. Finally, document the VM configuration and the snapshot ID; good notes make your experiments reproducible and defensible. What single VM configuration would you check first to ensure safety before executing a sample? Safe Dynamic Analysis: Preparing an Isolated VM means use isolated vms with snapshots, disabled host/network bridges, and simulated services to observe malware without risk.. In practical terms, essential steps to avoid cross-contamination and capture behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Static analysis gives you immediate, safe insight into a sample's structure. Begin with file-type identification using tools such as file on Linux or PEiD on Windows to determine format and detect common packers. Calculate hashes like SHA256 as the first IoC. Next, extract printable strings with tools like strings or FLOSS; these often reveal filenames, URLs, error messages, or A P I names and are quick wins. Inspect the import table and dependencies using Dependency Walker or Ghidra's import view to see which libraries are used—imports from ws2_32 are a hint the sample uses networking, while kernel32 imports suggest file system activity. If the import table is sparse or the binary is packed, suspect obfuscation and plan for unpacking. Finally, open the sample in a disassembler; even if code is obfuscated, function names, constants, and control-flow patterns convey important clues. A typical mistake is to stop at strings; while helpful, strings alone rarely prove functionality. Combine them with imports and disassembly to build a working hypothesis. Static Analysis Techniques and Tools means use file identifiers, string extraction, dependency viewers, and disassemblers to build an initial hypothesis about malware behavior.. In practical terms, file identification, strings, import tables, and packer detection. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Disassemblers convert machine code into assembly and sometimes pseudo-code, letting you inspect logical structure without needing source code. Tools like Ghidra and IDA Pro give you the ability to list imports, identify functions, and see call graphs that highlight suspicious routines. Start by loading the binary and looking at the import table to find networking and cryptography libraries; then find functions that call those imports. Use cross-references to map where data moves. An example: if you find a function that calls CreateFile, WriteFile, and then a cryptographic function, that sequence suggests file encryption behavior. A misconception is to rely entirely on automatic decompilation—decompilers can mislabel functions or produce incorrect pseudo-code for obfuscated binaries; use the assembly and cross-references to verify critical behavior. In practice, disassembly narrows your dynamic tests: pick a function to break on in a debugger or force specific inputs to watch how the code behaves at runtime. Which import would you prioritize for creating a focused dynamic test? Using Disassemblers: Ghidra & IDA means use imports and call graphs to locate suspect functions and validate decompiler output against assembly and cross-references.. In practical terms, how to inspect imports, functions, and control flow. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dynamic analysis reveals what malware actually does when executed. Once your isolated VM and monitoring tools are ready, execute the sample and capture process events, file and registry modifications, and network traffic. Use Process Monitor or Process Explorer to capture process creation, parent-child relationships, and any process injection behavior. Before you finish, keep three compact concepts in mind. First: static analysis is safe and fast, and it should be your starting point to collect hashes, strings, and import clues.
